---
title: "Version Control"
---

You have a project folder with a script and a data file in it. Right now,
the only history of that project is whatever you remember. This chapter
fixes that.

This is a **gentle** introduction — just enough to work safely day to day.
A deeper dive (branches, remotes, collaborating with a team on GitHub) comes
later in the book. For now: what git is, why it matters, how to install it,
enough command line to drive it, and the everyday workflow.

## What Git Is

Git is a tool that saves snapshots of a folder over time, on purpose, with
a note attached to each one.

If you've ever used "Track Changes" in Word, or kept files named
`report_v1.docx`, `report_v2.docx`, `report_FINAL.docx`,
`report_FINAL_really.docx` — you've already felt the problem git solves.
Instead of guessing which version is current, git keeps every saved
snapshot, labeled, in order, forever. You choose when to save a snapshot
(that's called a **commit**), and you write a short note explaining why.

A few terms you'll see everywhere:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Repository** (repo) | A project folder that git is tracking |
| **Commit** | A saved snapshot of the whole folder, plus a message |
| **Staging** | Choosing *which* changes go into the next commit |
| **History** | The full list of commits, oldest to newest |

## Why It's Important

**It's an audit trail.** Every commit records what changed, when, and why.
When someone asks "where did this number come from," you don't just show
the script — you show exactly which version of the script produced it.

**It's a safety net.** Made a change that broke everything? Every previous
commit is still there. You can always get back to a version that worked.

**It's how modern teams share code.** Emailing zip files back and forth
doesn't scale past one person. Git — paired with a hosting service like
GitHub — is how public health teams, CDC, and academic epi groups actually
collaborate on code today.

**It's expected of you.** Increasingly, "can you share your analysis" means
"can you share your repo." Knowing the basics is table stakes, not extra
credit.

## Installing Git

::: {.callout-tip}
## Install git before continuing

- **Windows:** download and run the installer from
  [git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com/downloads). Accept the defaults.
- **macOS:** open Terminal and run `git --version`. If it isn't already
  installed, macOS will prompt you to install the Xcode Command Line Tools —
  accept that.
- **Linux:** use your package manager, e.g. `sudo apt install git` (Debian/Ubuntu)
  or `sudo dnf install git` (Fedora).
:::

Once installed, confirm it worked:

```bash
git --version
```

You should see something like `git version 2.43.0`. Exact number doesn't
matter — any reasonably recent version is fine.

One-time setup, so your commits are labeled with your name:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

## Intro to the Command Line

Git's full power lives on the command line. RStudio and Positron both have
a **Terminal** tab/pane (next to the Console) — that's a command line
sitting right inside your IDE. Open it now; you'll use it for the rest of
this chapter.

A few commands you'll lean on, regardless of operating system:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `pwd` | Print working directory — where am I right now? |
| `ls` (`dir` on Windows) | List files in the current folder |
| `cd folder-name` | Change directory — move into `folder-name` |
| `cd ..` | Move up one level |

The terminal always has a **current location**, same idea as `here()` from
chapter 1 but for the shell instead of R. Before running git commands,
make sure you're inside your project folder:

```bash
cd covid-briefing
pwd
```

## The Happy Path Workflow

This is the loop you'll repeat, day in and day out. Five steps.

### 1. Turn a folder into a repository — once

Inside `covid-briefing/`:

```bash
git init
```

This creates a hidden `.git` folder. That's git's database — all your
history lives there. You only run `git init` once per project.

### 2. Check what's changed

```bash
git status
```

This is your most-used git command. It tells you what's new, what's
modified, and what git isn't tracking yet. Run it constantly — it never
changes anything, it only reports.

### 3. Stage the changes you want to save

```bash
git add scripts/01_import.R
```

Staging means "include this file in the *next* commit." You can stage one
file, several, or everything:

```bash
git add .
```

`git add .` stages every changed file in the current folder and below. Fine
for now — the difference between staging some files versus all of them
matters more once you're working with others, which is a further-reading
topic.

### 4. Commit — save the snapshot

```bash
git commit -m "Import raw COVID data and inspect structure"
```

The `-m` flag attaches your message right there. Write it like you're
telling a colleague what you did and why — future you *is* that colleague.

### 5. Review the history

```bash
git log
```

This lists every commit: who, when, and the message. `git log --oneline`
gives you a compact one-line-per-commit view once your history grows.

::: {.callout-note}
## The mental model

Three places your work can live: the **working directory** (files on
disk, as you're editing them), the **staging area** (what you've marked
for the next commit with `git add`), and the **repository** (committed
history, safe in `.git`). `git status` tells you what's in each. `git add`
moves changes to staging. `git commit` moves staging into history.
:::

### Putting it together

A normal working session looks like this:

```bash
git status               # see what changed
git add data/processed/  # stage the files you want to save
git status                # confirm what's staged
git commit -m "Clean town names and drop test rows"
git log --oneline         # confirm it landed
```

Repeat that loop every time you reach a working, meaningful checkpoint —
not just at the end of the day. Small, frequent commits with clear
messages are worth far more later than one giant commit called "updates."
